title: How to Think When You're Torn About Changing Jobs | Sorting Out Your Decision Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone torn between wanting to change jobs and having reasons to stay at their current workplace. A look at what's behind the indecision, ways to sort it out, how to read the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself.
h1: When you're torn about changing jobs
lead: Feeling "I want to quit" and "will it really be okay if I quit?" at the same time doesn't make you indecisive. A job is a choice where income, relationships, self-worth, and your outlook for the future are all tangled together at once, so it's natural to feel torn. On this page, we'll break down the decision you're torn over about changing jobs, and introduce tarot cards that reflect each angle.

sections.p: Being torn about changing jobs is often a tug-of-war between "dissatisfaction with where you are now" and "anxiety about what's next." When the dissatisfaction is strong, you want to decide on impulse; when the anxiety is strong, you lean toward staying put. Both are honest feelings, but deciding on one alone tends to lead to regret. Reluctance to let go of what you've built up — "but I've worked so hard to get here" — and worrying about what people around you will think also weigh on the decision. Start by putting what's inside this indecision into words, writing out the dissatisfaction, anxiety, reluctance, and hopes separately, and you'll start to see what is pulling you the most.

The key to sorting it out is to think separately about "what you want to move away from" and "what you want to move toward." If you move only for the reasons you want to leave, you may meet the same problem at your next workplace. On the other hand, if what you want to move toward is clear, you'll also see the option of setting a preparation period and moving in stages. Check the practical side, too: could you get by if your income stopped for a few months, and is there really nothing left you could still try at your current job? Once you've lined up both your feelings and the conditions, imagining "which choice would I feel at peace with six months from now" makes it easier to find your footing.

When you're torn about changing jobs, cards that stand for "leaving," "starting something new," and "stopping to take another look" can offer clues. The Eight of Cups shows someone walking away, by their own choice, from a place that still looks fulfilling. The Fool points to the courage to take a step forward even when your preparation isn't complete, and the Seven of Pentacles points to the stance of calmly weighing the fruits of your efforts so far. The cards don't decide the answer for you; they are a mirror that lights up which stage you are at right now. Look at whether the card you drew leans toward "moving" or toward "taking another look," and compare it with how you honestly feel.

As for income and your outlook for daily life, how much security do you need, at a minimum, to feel at ease? A year from now, which version of you — the one who chose which option — could say "I'm glad I made that move back then"? If there's a question you can't answer, that's the point you should look into or talk to someone about next. Breaking what you're torn about into small questions is a shortcut to a decision you can accept.

title: How to Think When You're Torn During a Job Hunt | Sorting Out Your Path Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone whose job hunt has them torn — you can't settle on an industry, you can't decide which offer to accept, or the selection process isn't going well. A look at what's behind the indecision, ways to sort it out, the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself.
h1: When you're torn during a job hunt
lead: While everyone around you receives offers one after another, you feel like you're the only one being left behind. You don't know what you want to do, and meanwhile the deadlines for application forms just keep getting closer. The indecision in a job hunt comes from the pressure of having to make your first step into working life the "right answer." On this page, we'll look at ways to sort out what you're torn about in your job hunt, and tarot cards that reflect those angles.

sections.p: Much of the indecision in a job hunt comes from the anxiety of "I don't know what I want to do" and the assumption that "I can't afford to fail." It can feel as if your first company will decide your whole life, which makes the choice feel heavier than it needs to be. It's also characteristic of job hunting that other people's yardsticks slip in easily — friends' offers, parents' expectations, how well-known a company is. Every time you're turned down in a selection process, it can feel as if you yourself were rejected, and your confidence drops. Start by separating the voices around you from your own honest feelings, and writing down what exactly you're torn about.

What helps you sort things out is to start not from "what you want to do" but from "what you want to value." Even if you can't yet picture the work itself, you can find conditions you won't give up: wanting to work with people, wanting to learn a trade, wanting a stable environment. If you're torn between several offers, writing the conditions down and ranking them makes it harder to be swept along by feelings alone. It also matters to know that your first choice doesn't decide everything. You may discover your aptitudes only once you're working, and a career can be rebuilt any number of times.

When you're torn in a job hunt, cards that stand for "outlook," "beginnings," "steady accumulation," "holding your ground," and "moving forward" can offer clues. The Three of Wands shows a figure looking out from high ground across the sea, waiting for the possibilities ahead. The Magician points to the power to start acting with the tools already in your hands, and the Eight of Pentacles points to the stance of honing your skills one by one. The Seven of Wands stands for the persistence to protect your position even in an unfavorable situation, and The Chariot stands for the power to move forward with intention, even while you still feel torn. Check which stage you are at now — preparation, challenge, or decision.

title: How to Think When You're Torn About Starting a Side Job | Sorting Out Your Way of Working Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone who wants to start a side job but is torn — wondering whether they'll have the time and energy, whether it will affect their main job, or what they should even do. A look at what's behind the indecision, ways to sort it out, the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself.
h1: When you're torn about starting a side job
lead: You want another source of income, and you'd like to try something different from your main job. But you can't quite get started, because you worry whether your time and energy will hold out, and whether it will affect your main job. Being torn over a side job is a question of how to balance a new possibility against your life as it is now. On this page, we'll look at ways to sort things out when you're torn about starting a side job, and tarot cards that reflect those angles.

sections.p: Much of the indecision over a side job is a standoff between the feeling of "I want to try it" and the anxiety of "can I really keep it up?" You're already tired from your main job — can you really spend even more time? Will it go against company rules, and what will people think? Not knowing what to start with, you can also end up spending all your time just gathering information. Wariness of deals that sound too good, and the fear that you might start and earn nothing, also drag the indecision out. Start by putting into words what you want to get from a side job — income, skills, or a sense of fulfillment.

What helps you sort things out is the idea of "starting small, and finding a form you can keep up." Rather than aiming for a large income from the start, beginning with something you can do in a few hours a week lets you move forward while checking the effect on your main job and your life. Before you start, it will reassure you to check whether your work rules allow side jobs, and to look into how taxes such as the final tax return are handled. The experience you've built up in your current job or hobbies may also be of use to someone just as it is. As well as learning something entirely new, consider the path of making use of abilities you already have.

When you're torn over a side job, cards that stand for "steady accumulation," "balancing two things," "beginnings," "outlook," "cooperation," and "overlooking something" can offer clues. The Eight of Pentacles shows someone carefully building up their work piece by piece, honing their craft. The Two of Pentacles points to the sense of balance in skillfully keeping two things going at once, and The Magician points to the will to start something with the abilities in your hands. The Three of Wands stands for the viewpoint of looking out over what lies beyond, the Three of Pentacles stands for the power to give something shape by working with others, and the Four of Cups stands for a state in which you haven't noticed an opportunity being offered to you. Check whether what you need right now is preparation or action.

title: How to Think When You're Torn About Going Independent or Starting a Business | Sorting Out the Challenge Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone torn about leaving their company to go independent, or starting a business of their own. A look at what's behind the indecision, between the wish to take on the challenge and anxiety about stability, plus ways to sort it out, the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself.
h1: When you're torn about going independent or starting a business
lead: You want to run a business under your own power, and choose how you work outside an organization. At the same time, there's the fear of your income drying up, and the anxiety that if you fail, there's no going back. Being torn over independence or starting a business is a question of which to put first: the challenge, or stability. On this page, we'll look at ways to sort out what you're torn about when you carve out a path of your own, and tarot cards that reflect those angles.

sections.p: Being torn over independence or starting a business is a tug-of-war between "hopes for what's possible" and "fear of failure." Hearing stories of people who succeeded can make you feel you could do it too, while the anxiety swells — what if my income disappears, what if people think I failed? There's also reluctance to let go of the stability and title of being an employee, and of the protected environment. And when your picture of the business is still vague and you don't know where to begin, the indecision drags on. Start by putting into words why you want to go independent — is the motive freedom, income, or a sense of fulfillment?

What helps you sort things out is not thinking in terms of "all or nothing." You can prepare in stages: try the business on a small scale before you quit and check how it feels, or line up prospects for your first clients in advance. Deciding on concrete yardsticks — how many months of living expenses in savings would make you feel secure, how much in sales you would need to foresee before taking the plunge — makes it harder to be swept around by emotion. It also matters to look for where what you're good at and what people are asking for overlap. Only when both are in place — something you want to do, and people willing to pay for it — does it work as a business.

When you're torn over going independent or starting a business, cards that stand for "planning," "independence," "burden," and "opportunity" can offer clues. The Two of Wands shows a figure gazing at a globe in their hand, planning where to head next. The Nine of Pentacles points to abundance and independence built by your own power, and the Ten of Wands points to the danger of carrying too much alone. The Fool stands for the courage to accept uncertainty and step onto a new path, and the Ace of Pentacles stands for a practical opportunity that has appeared in front of you. title: How to Think When You're Torn About Further Study or Relearning | Sorting Out Your Choice Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone torn over choosing where to study, or an adult relearning or gaining a qualification. Is it worth the time and money? A look at what's behind the indecision, ways to sort it out, the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself.
h1: When you're torn about further study or relearning
lead: Learning is an investment in your future, but it takes time, money, and energy. Can you still make it if you start now? Will it really be useful? Can you keep it up? Being torn over further study or relearning holds just as much hope as anxiety. On this page, we'll look at ways to sort out choices about learning, and tarot cards that reflect those angles.

sections.p: Much of the indecision over learning is a clash between "the wish to do it" and "the calculation of whether it's worth the investment." You're interested, but when you think of the fees and the time, you can't take the step. A qualification feels as if it might open a path, yet there's also the anxiety that you might gain it and never use it. Awareness of your age and comparisons — feeling you're behind everyone else, or that it's too late to start now — also weigh on the decision. When choosing where to study, test scores and reputation and family opinions get mixed in, and you can lose sight of what you yourself want to learn. Start by writing down, in your own words, why you want to learn.

The key to sorting it out is to think about the "purpose" of the learning and its "form" separately. What you should choose depends on whether the purpose is to use it in your work, pure interest, or regaining confidence. As for the form, there is more than one option: attending a school, learning by correspondence, or trying it on your own. Before investing heavily all at once, trying a short course or a book lets you check whether it fits you. And if you picture concretely the situations in which, having finished learning, you would use that knowledge, it becomes easier to judge the value of the investment.

The Page of Pentacles, in the figure of a young person gazing intently at the coin in their hand, shows the stance of facing new learning with sincerity. title: How to Think When You're Torn About Leaving Your Job | Sorting Out Your Decision Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone torn about quitting their job. Through what's really behind your reasons for wanting to leave, the money and next steps to sort out before you resign, the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself, here are some hints for thinking through whether to leave or stay.
h1: When you're torn about leaving your job
lead: Sunday night. Just thinking about going to the office tomorrow morning makes your chest feel heavy. Lying in bed, you grip your phone, search "I want to quit," and quietly close it again. You want to leave, yet when it comes to actually leaving, your feet freeze. How many months have you carried this indecision? For some people, years. Let me say this first: the goal of this page is not "to decide tonight whether to leave or stay." The goal is to reach a morning where, whichever you choose, you can feel "I decided without regret." What you do tonight, to that end, is not deciding — it's bringing the "I want to quit" that's been going around in your head out into the open. Decisions are what your morning mind does best.

sections.p: When you're torn about leaving, the hardship rarely has a single source. Is it the relationships, the work itself, how you're evaluated or paid, or the limits of your physical strength? Bundling it into the big phrase "I hate this company" hides the real problem. The strength of the wish to quit also changes from day to day. On a day with a bad meeting it can feel like your limit, yet after a break you may feel somewhat recovered. That very wavering makes you doubt yourself — "is this really worth quitting over?" — and postpones the decision. Another part is the fear of the blank space after you leave: no next job decided yet, a period with no income, a gap in your résumé. Often the problem is less the current job itself than anxiety about that unknown period.

What you do tonight is write down just three reasons you want to quit. But don't try to sort them out only inside your head. Writing while you look at a card you've drawn makes it easier to separate "reasons that are truly your own" from "reasons influenced by the voices around you." The card you drew is not for producing an answer; use it as a mirror that reflects your current state. Once you've written them down, divide them into "things that would be solved by a change of environment" and "things that would follow you wherever you go." A boss or a commute is an environment problem, but how you choose work, or being unable to say no, may repeat at the next workplace too. Line up the practical side of money in the same place. How many months could you live with no income? From when, and how much, would unemployment benefits come in? Once you can see the numbers, anxiety changes from "something frightening" into "a period to get through." If you keep what you wrote in a log, you can look back on it later. The results of small steps you tried before quitting — asking for a transfer, taking a leave of absence, discussing your workload — also become, if kept in the log, proof of "a decision made after thinking it through." This is the mechanism by which the months you spent feeling torn finally pay off.

When you're torn about leaving, cards that stand for "drawing a line," "recovery," and "steady accumulation" can offer clues. The Eight of Cups shows someone quietly leaving a place that no longer fulfills their heart. It reflects the resolve to draw a line under your current job. The Four of Swords is a knight lying down to rest in the middle of the fight. It may be a sign that before any decision, you first need recovery. The Wheel of Fortune shows a timing when the flow changes. It asks not only about your own will, but about the turn of timing as well. The Eight of Pentacles is a craftsperson steadily honing their skill. It makes you think about whether what you've built up in your current place is an asset that will serve you in the next one too. The Fool is a young person standing at the edge of a cliff with a single bundle. Rather than a leap with zero preparation, it reminds you of the possibility of "starting over lightly."

title: How to Think When You're Torn About Taking Time Off Work | Sorting It Out Through the Lens of Tarot
description: For anyone torn about taking time off work, who ends up going in even when they feel unwell. Through what's really behind the reasons you can't rest, the material for judging whether to rest or go in, the related tarot cards, and questions to ask yourself, here are some hints for deciding how to take your rest.
h1: When you're torn about taking time off work
lead: You feel feverish, yet your hand stops before making the call to say you'll be absent. "Maybe I can manage today." "If I take the day off, I'll cause trouble for others." Paid leave exists as a right, yet every time you use it, a small guilt comes with it. Let me say this first: whether to rest is not a question of willpower, but a question of judgment that looks at both your condition and your work. This page guides you through how to line up the material for that judgment.

sections.p: There are broadly three reasons you feel torn and unable to rest. The first is worry about troubling the people around you. Your share of the work shifts to someone else. That worry itself is fair — but have you compared it with the burden if you push yourself and make things drag on? The second is anxiety about how you'll be evaluated. Will resting look like slacking off? In reality, there are fewer situations than you might think where pushing through illness is what gets evaluated well. The third is how loosely you judge your own condition. If your standard for "I'm still okay" has been raised to just before you collapse, the judgment to rest will always come late. Once you see what's behind the indecision, the judgment changes from a question of permission — "may I rest?" — to a question of material — "would resting be better for everyone overall?"

Line up the material. For your body, there are four: fever, sleep, appetite, and concentration. For your work: whether there is anything that must happen today, and whether it's in a form that can be handed over. Writing both out, you'll find that the "reasons I should go in" are surprisingly lacking in concreteness. If you rest, it also helps to decide the form of your message in advance. That you'll be absent, the handover for today's matters, and a rough idea of when you'll return — those three points are enough. This sorting out goes more easily if you do it while looking at a card you've drawn. The card is not there to tell you to rest; it's a mirror that reflects your current state — whether you're close to your limit, or moving out of guilt. If you keep a log of the days you rested and the days you went in, you'll start to see your own pattern of pushing too hard.

When you're torn about resting, cards that stand for "rest," "recovery," "limits," "balance," and "weariness" can offer clues. The Four of Swords shows a knight lying down with his swords set aside. It shows that stepping away from the field of battle to rest is itself preparation for your next action. The Hermit is a sage standing alone with a lantern. sections.p: At the center of being torn over getting back together is "nostalgia." Happy memories don't fade, while the pain of the parting thins with time, so the past looks more beautiful than it actually was. The anxiety of new encounters, and the loneliness of being alone, can also push forward the feeling that "after all, that person was the one." However, there was always a reason for the breakup. If that reason remains now, the possibility of stumbling in the same place even if you go back stays high. Start by writing out, separately, the nostalgic feelings, the loneliness, your lingering attachment to the other person, and the reasons you broke up.

The key to sorting it out is to distinguish "is what I want to return to the person themselves, or the sense of security of those days?" Check whether you can concretely picture a future spent with them, and whether the problem that became the reason for breaking up is likely to actually change between the two of you. It's not only your own feelings that matter, but the other person's situation and feelings too. Whether to get in touch can be thought of separately from getting back together itself. Exchanging small updates can become material for knowing where the two of you stand now. On the other hand, the choice to prioritize time to rebuild your own life is just as important. Without rushing to a conclusion, there are also things that come into view by taking time.

When you're torn over getting back together, cards that reflect "longing for the past," "looking back and facing it again," and "accepting an ending" can offer clues. The Six of Cups stands for nostalgic memories, and longing for the peace of the past. Judgement shows the figure of looking back on the past, and facing feelings and a relationship that had been sleeping, once more. Death shows that by properly ending one ending, the next thing begins. Look at whether the card you drew leans toward "returning" or toward "ending," and lay it over your own honest feelings.

sections.p: Try answering the following questions. Is what you want to return to the person themselves, or the sense of security of those days? Could the two of you, as you are now, overcome the reasons you broke up? Can you concretely picture a future spent with the other person? Is what you're torn about now something that only appears at times when your loneliness is strong? Which choice — the one that went back, or the one that moved forward — is the you of six months from now likely to look back on more calmly? Having looked at both the past and the future, choose with your own feet.
